topic: What if humans could breathe underwater, but only for ten seconds?
title: WHAT IF YOU COULD
BREATHE UNDERWATER?

power.rule: you can breathe underwater, but every breath runs out after exactly ten seconds
power.look: three cyan gill slits at the neck, a cooling blue grade, a BREATHE chip and a wrist dial counting 10 to 0

script.text: Grab a coin. Breathe. Still under.
Race your friend. Breathe. He stops at ten.
What if you could breathe underwater, ten seconds at a time?

script.beat: 4 the turn: the cost, one real fact
script.text: One catch: a liter of water holds about nine milligrams of oxygen. Even with perfect gills, you need forty liters a minute. That's real.
So what happens at second eleven?

science.claim: A liter of air-saturated freshwater at 20 °C holds about nine milligrams of dissolved oxygen.
science.working: Published saturation values at 20 °C and sea level: 9.06 mg/L (Wisconsin DNR DO table), 9.077 mg/L (FAO/EIFAC table), 9.1 ppm (NC State Extension). Rounded to about 9 mg/L in the script and on the schematic.
science.source: Wisconsin DNR, BOD101 DO saturation table; FAO, Water Quality & Aquaculture manual, Table I (EIFAC 1986); NC State Extension, Dissolved Oxygen Saturation in Fresh Water

science.claim: A resting adult uses about 250 milliliters of oxygen a minute, so even with perfect gills you would need roughly forty liters of water a minute.
science.working: Resting oxygen consumption: 200-250 mL/min (ACE, 2018) and 250-350 mL/min (Dominelli et al., 2021); use 250 mL/min. At STP, 1 mol of gas is 22.4 L, so 0.250/22.4 = 0.0112 mol O2/min = 0.0112 x 32 g/mol = 0.357 g = 357 mg O2/min. At 9 mg O2/L, 357/9 = 39.7 L of water per minute, assuming 100 percent extraction; real fish gills extract up to about 80 percent, which would require more flow. The schematic states about 40 L/min.
science.source: ACE Fitness, January 2018 (resting 200-250 mL O2/min); Dominelli et al., 2021, PMC8026750 (250-350 mL/min at rest); O2 molar volume 22.4 L/mol; dissolved-oxygen tables above

shots.note: dusk cove: Pip runs in and dives, the low sun in frame
underwater, Pip glides down through a shaft of sun; gill slits glow, bubbles rise
a school of silver fish scatters above his head
an old gold coin half-buried in sand; a mitten grabs it
Pip holds up the coin, grinning; the wrist dial counts down
Pip and Mo race across the reef, Pip a length ahead
Mo stops dead as his dial hits zero; Pip streaks past blurred
the premise over the cove at dusk; Pip surfaces with the coin
the wrist dial snaps from 10 to 0, then resets to 10
a one-liter glass of water on a blueprint grid, with nine tiny oxygen dots
a label reads 9 mg O2 per liter; the dots drift in the glass
lungs pull 250 mL O2 a minute; forty liters of water per minute counts up
Pip, worried; the blue light turns cold, his gills flicker
the sun shafts die, a long shadow moves in the dark beyond him
